Read the mechanism

One rotating face, one opposing face

The rotor turns the shaft, lower carrier and lower burr together. The upper burr stays fixed during grinding. The model shows the same angular phase for the shaft and lower burr.

The center feeds the cutting region

The hopper funnel directs beans into the central opening. The opposing teeth fracture the beans. Fragments travel outward toward the finer cutting region and leave through the chute.

A cutaway is not transparency

Each section removes a geometric region. The model exposes the remaining surfaces and closes the cut faces. Orbit toward the rear to see how the solid housing hides the internals.

Interpret the technical details

The gap and the particle distribution differ

A smaller gap generally produces finer grounds. Coffee still fractures into a distribution of sizes. Burr geometry, alignment, bean properties and operating conditions also affect the result.

Alignment is a tolerance stack

Shaft location, bearing support, carrier seating and burr mounting combine at the working faces. Errors in those interfaces change the clearance around the rim. This model keeps the two burr faces parallel.

Try a useful comparison

Select Motor. Hover the rotor, stator, shaft and bearing. Then start the motor at teaching speed. The rotor and shaft turn. The stator stays fixed. Select Burr pair to compare the two cutting faces.

Model boundaries, controls and sources

What is verified

Eureka lists 55 mm hardened-steel flat burrs, an AC motor, 1,350 rpm and 310 W absorbed power for this reference. Eureka describes the micrometric adjustment as lower-burr repositioning.

What is illustrative

All internal dimensions use model units. The apparent motor air gap, pole count, winding turns, bearing races, carrier geometry and adjustment travel are not factory specifications. The tooth layout explains coarse and fine cutting regions, not a specific burr drawing.

The operating gap, motor speed and inspection travel each come from one shared model. The rotor, shaft and lower burr share the same angular phase. The upper assembly does not rotate.

Camera and accessibility controls

Drag to orbit through 360 degrees. Use the wheel or zoom buttons for close inspection. Use right-drag to pan. Fit view restores the camera. The labels keep their text size during zoom.

Hover a visible part to inspect it. Use the part selector for a hidden part. Click a label or select Retain selection to keep its details during camera motion. Release selection restores hover updates.

Reduced motion keeps the mechanism still while it preserves orbit, zoom, cutaways and hover. Enable animation explicitly overrides that preference for this page. The animation stops outside the viewport.

Inside the Comandante C40.

A separate 3D teaching model of the C40 MK4 Nitro Blade with a standard axle and a 44 mm oak knob.
Orbit, zoom, expose individual assemblies, and hover the parts. Dimensions and unpublished internals are illustrative.

2Documented bearing cartridges
3Independent click-lock ball units
73Inspectable elements / not a factory BOM
Standard adjustmentNot the optional Red Clix axle

The manufacturer documents the assemblies and their roles. This original illustration approximates dimensions, teeth, threads, bearing internals and small retainers. It does not reproduce factory CAD or a complete factory bill of materials. The optional legacy O-ring is absent by default. The collected grounds and their sizes are illustrative.

Follow the torque and reaction paths

The hand turns the crank. The axle transfers that motion to the inner cone. The outer ring stays fixed in the body. The user's other hand resists the body's reaction torque.

The knob travels around the axle while its own pin allows a pivot. The model keeps the knob's world orientation steady to illustrate this freedom. The lid follows its press-fit crank attachment.

Separate rotation from axial support

The two bearings locate the axle. The raised side of each spacer washer faces its bearing. The lower washer and spring form the cone's preload path.

The cutaway exposes generic races, a cage and eight balls in each cartridge. Only the two-cartridge arrangement is a manufacturer specification. Ball count, cage speed and internal profiles are illustrative.

Change the cone position, not the ring

The three-legged dial engages the standard threaded axle. Three independent steel-ball units hold the selected relative position. A higher click count lowers the cone and opens the depicted gap.

For example, change 24 clicks to 25. The model lowers the cone by 0.14 model units. This value is an illustration, not a micrometer-per-click specification. The display does not convert the gap into particle diameter.

Understand the floating cone

The manufacturer describes limited cone freedom when the grinder is empty. Coffee load centers the cone during grinding. The optional unloaded-play control illustrates this freedom without claiming a measured amplitude.

Two concepts differ: shaft support and cone constraint. This distinction forms the model's ★ kinematic coupling ★. For example, the bearings can locate the shaft while the cone retains a small freedom at its interface.

What this model does not specify

This model does not specify factory dimensions, burr microblade geometry, thread pitch, spring force, bearing ball count or particle-size distribution. Its inspection offsets are explanatory, not a service procedure. The outer-ring screws remain fixed.

The glass jar appears as an opaque cutaway for clarity. The supplied polymer jar is an alternative, not a second installed collection chamber. The scene uses a manufacturer-standard natural oak knob. Cosmetic variants and optional Red Clix or Gold Clix systems are outside this model.
